 China eases its 'South Korea ban,' opening the door to the Hallyu wave after 10 years?
 South Korea and China have reached an agreement to ensure that Korean content receives fair scrutiny in China, while also expanding opportunities for cooperation in film and television production. However, Kpop performances remain restricted, so this agreement does not mean that the entire Hallyu wave will be free to return to the Chinese market, Chosun reported on November 18.
 Báo Thanh niên • 19/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Chinese President Xi Jinping have officially announced the completion of further negotiations on the Korea-China Free Trade Agreement (FTA), including in the areas of services and investment. This development has drawn attention from the cultural industry to the possibility of the two countries making progress on the issue of restricting Hallyu (the Korean Wave).
 The agreement expands opportunities for cooperation between South Korea and China. 
 China implemented "Korean restrictions" starting in 2016, after South Korea decided to deploy the THAAD missile defense system. While not publicly issuing a ban, the country is believed to have secretly directed domestic television stations, entertainment companies, and platforms, preventing Korean artists from appearing on Chinese television or being hired as advertising faces. Korean K-pop concerts, films, and dramas were also restricted from import and broadcast. Even global stars like BTS were unable to hold their Arirang tour in mainland China. Member Suga once expressed his regret, saying, "Korean singers have no way to perform in China." 
 Despite their global influence, BTS has yet to have the opportunity to bring their concerts to audiences in mainland China.
 Photo: Reuters
 You may also like However, according to the South Korean Ministry of Industry, Trade and Resources and the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, the new agreement ensures that South Korean online games, films, and other content receive "most-favored-nation treatment" during China's pre-approval process. This principle aims to ensure that South Korean content is not treated unfairly compared to content from third countries.
 The scope of collaborative content production has also been expanded. Previously, co-production was limited to feature films. Under the new agreement, projects can include television dramas, animation, entertainment programs, and documentaries, thereby broadening opportunities for collaboration between Korean producers and Chinese businesses.
 Kpop is still unable to return to the Chinese stage. 
 While this agreement benefits the content sector, including films and television dramas, it does not mean that restrictions on Hallyu will be lifted immediately or that the Chinese K-pop market will be opened up.
 You may also like The "most-favored-nation" principle and non-discriminatory review only ensure that Korean content is not treated less favorably than content from third countries like the US or Japan . This does not mean that content will be automatically approved, as it will still have to go through China's strict censorship process. The agreement also does not include specific provisions on resuming commercial performances by Korean artists. Since the restrictions on Hallyu were implemented... Under the new regulations, commercial Kpop concerts in mainland China are strictly banned; performances are only permitted in Hong Kong and Macau. Even when events are held, only Chinese or foreign artists are allowed to perform, while Korean artists remain prohibited.
 In other words, the new agreement is just the starting point for cultural exchange between the two countries, and the possibility of the Kpop market being opened up remains unclear. Industry representatives believe that careful monitoring of administrative procedures is necessary, such as licensing live performances, visa issuance, and obtaining permits from local authorities. They also emphasize the need to ensure that events can take place freely without interference from authorities.
 Another unresolved issue is the potential political barriers that may arise. Even if Hallyu artists are allowed to perform in China, those who do not support the "One China" policy or advocate for independence for Taiwan or Hong Kong may still face restrictions.
